Safeguards — privilege boundary and operator console

Why the application never runs as root, how privileged work is reached through a queue instead of a function call, and the guards built into the satom operator console.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereServer side (service account, privileged update runner); the satom console on the node
On this page
  • The privilege boundary
  • The operator console

The privilege boundary#

The application does not run as root. What needs root is reached through a queue, not a function call.

Guard What it prevents
Dedicated unprivileged service account with a short sudo allowlist The web application holding root. Its sudo grants are an explicit short list (for example, testing and reloading the web server configuration), never ALL.
Account pinned in a systemd drop-in, not in the shipped unit A self-update that replaces unit files silently handing the application root again.
Privileged runner triggered by a watched request directory The web process passing a command to root. It can only submit a typed request; the runner decides what that request means.
Role probe that works unprivileged High-availability guards silently taking the "not primary" branch. The obvious role probe needs root and, run unprivileged, returns empty — which once made guards skip their work while the service reported success. Every HA guard now probes the node's role through a path that answers correctly at any privilege level.
The console is never granted to the service account Root by another name. A password-less sudo rule for the satom console for the service account would be equivalent to unrestricted sudo; the console's privilege diagnostic fails loudly if it finds such a rule.

The operator console#

The satom console is a tool for the node whose web interface is the thing that broke. Everything about it follows from that requirement — and from the fact that it is run with elevated privilege.

Guard What it prevents
No framework imports at module level A diagnostic that cannot run when the installation is broken. Commands that genuinely need the application import it inside the function and degrade with a stated reason. The test suite checks this by parsing the source, because a stray import would not be noticed until the day it matters.
A root-owned copy outside the application tree Privilege escalation through the tool itself. The application tree is owned by the service account; a launcher that ran code from it would let a compromised web worker rewrite what an administrator runs under sudo. The installer verifies owner and mode, and refuses a symlink.
Re-installed after every update A stale console. The copy lives outside the tree, so a code update does not reach it on its own — the installer, the update runner and a repair command all refresh it.
Refusal instead of a traceback An operator guessing. A state-changing command run without privilege prints permission denied: with the full command line, arguments included, and exits with its own code (3). Retyping remembered arguments is how the wrong ones get typed.
Read commands never write A diagnostic that creates the drift it reports. Repository status runs without optional locks, and byte-code writing is disabled during a compile check, because both were silently taking ownership of files away from the service account.
Destructive commands must be declared An irreversible action with no confirmation. Destructive commands exit with a usage error unless --yes is given, and a command marked destructive that does not require confirmation fails the test suite.
The command tree is data, not code paths A command with no help text or no declared privilege class. The parser, help, completion, privilege gate and JSON output all read one structure, and an incomplete entry breaks the build.
The output path cannot crash Dying while printing. Colour and decoration are stripped when output goes to a pipe, box-drawing and typographic characters fold to ASCII on terminals that cannot show them, and the output stream replaces anything it cannot encode — a hostname, a certificate subject, a log line. A serial console once killed a command over a dash in a title.
Refuses to control its own runner Re-entering the privilege boundary sideways. The privileged update runner and the database engine cannot be started, stopped or restarted from the console. Disabling the runner is refused outright, because every queued update would then sit pending with nothing reporting it.

ℹ️Note — The runner can still be re-armed

The console refuses to disable the privileged runner, but satom execute enable updater is allowed — it is the documented fix when updates sit queued because the runner's trigger is not enabled. Enable it on both nodes.

💡Tip — Console exit codes

0 success · 1 the command ran and the result is bad · 2 usage error (including a destructive command without --yes) · 3 insufficient privilege · 4 the command could not run (missing dependency, no credentials). See Operator CLI.

#root#sudo#service account#privilege#systemd drop-in#update runner#request queue#satom#cli#console#destructive#--yes#exit code
